Up to now a matrix has been a table of numbers that you multiply and row-reduce. This post changes the point of view: a matrix is only a description of a linear map, written in one particular pair of bases. Change the bases and the same map gets a different matrix. That idea explains why rank, trace and determinant are "real" properties of a map while individual entries are not, and it is the doorway to eigenvalues in the next post. The second half of the post builds the determinant from three simple rules, proves the key facts (product rule, invertibility test, Cramer's rule), and shows what the number means geometrically: the factor by which a map scales area or volume, with a sign for orientation.
Series map: 00 Vectors & Linear Systems → 01 Matrix Algebra, Inverses & LU → 02 Vector Spaces, Basis & Dimension → 03 Linear Maps, Change of Basis & Determinants (this post) → 04 Eigenvalues & Diagonalization → 05 Inner Products, Spectral Theorem & SVD.

Decide whether a given function between vector spaces is linear, and find its kernel and image.
State and prove the rank–nullity theorem for linear maps, and use it to relate injective, surjective and invertible.
Write the matrix of a linear map relative to any bases, and explain why composition of maps is the matrix product.
Convert coordinates between bases, and compute the matrix of a map in a new basis with P−1AP.
Recognise rotations, reflections, shears, projections and scalings in R2 from their matrices.
Define the determinant by its three axioms, compute it by cofactor expansion and by elimination, and prove det⁡(AB)=det⁡Adet⁡B.
Interpret ∣det⁡A∣ as a volume scaling factor and the sign of det⁡A as orientation.
Solve small systems with Cramer's rule, and explain why it is not used for large ones.

Vector space V over R — as in Linear Algebra 02: a set with addition and scalar multiplication obeying the eight axioms. Everything in this post also works over C or any field.
Linear map (linear transformation) T:V→W — a function that respects addition and scalar multiplication (definition below). When V=W it is also called a linear operator on V.
Domain V and codomain W — where inputs live and where outputs are allowed to land.
Kernel (null space) ker⁡T={v∈V:T(v)=0}.
Image (range) im⁡T={T(v):v∈V}.
Rank of T — dim⁡im⁡T. Nullity of T — dim⁡ker⁡T.
Injective (one-to-one) — T(u)=T(v) implies u=v. Surjective (onto) — im⁡T=W. Bijective — both.
Isomorphism — a bijective linear map. V and W are isomorphic, written V≅W, if an isomorphism exists.
Pn — polynomials of degree at most n with real coefficients; dim⁡Pn=n+1.

A function T:V→W is linear if for all u,v∈V and all scalars c:
T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v),T(cv)=c T(v).
The two conditions combine into one: T(c1v1+c2v2)=c1T(v1)+c2T(v2). By induction, a linear map sends every linear combination to the same combination of the images. Taking c=0 gives T(0)=0: a linear map always sends zero to zero.
Examples:
Matrix maps. For an m×n matrix A, the map TA:Rn→Rm, TA(x)=Ax, is linear because A(u+v)=Au+Av and A(cv)=cAv (Linear Algebra 01).
Differentiation. D:P3→P2, D(p)=p′. The sum rule and the constant-multiple rule of calculus are exactly the two linearity conditions.
Integration. I:C[0,1]→R, I(f)=∫01f(x) dx, where C[0,1] is the space of continuous functions on [0,1].
Evaluation. E:P2→R2, E(p)=(p(0),p(1)).
Transpose. M↦MT from m×n matrices to n×m matrices.
Non-examples:
Translation T(x)=x+b with b≠0: T(0)=b≠0, so it is not linear. (It is called affine.)
T(x,y)=(x+y,xy): T(2⋅(1,1))=(4,4) but 2 T(1,1)=(4,2).
T(x)=∣x∣ on R: T(−1)=1≠−T(1).
Trick: To show a map is not linear, one counterexample is enough — and checking T(0)=0 first catches many cases in one line. To show a map is linear, you must check both conditions for arbitrary inputs.

Theorem 1. Let b1,…,bn be a basis of V and let w1,…,wn be any vectors in W. There is exactly one linear map T:V→W with T(bi)=wi for every i.
Proof. Every v∈V has unique coordinates: v=c1b1+⋯+cnbn (Linear Algebra 02). Define T(v)=c1w1+⋯+cnwn. This is well defined because the coordinates are unique. It is linear: if v has coordinates ci and u has coordinates di, then u+v has coordinates ci+di and kv has coordinates kci, and the formula is linear in the coordinates. It sends bi to wi. For uniqueness, any linear S with S(bi)=wi satisfies S(v)=∑ciS(bi)=∑ciwi=T(v). ∎
This theorem is the reason matrices work at all: to store a linear map you only need to store n vectors, the images of the basis vectors.

Proposition 2. For linear T:V→W, ker⁡T is a subspace of V and im⁡T is a subspace of W.
Proof. T(0)=0, so 0 is in both. If T(u)=T(v)=0 then T(u+cv)=0+c⋅0=0, so the kernel is closed under addition and scaling. If w1=T(v1) and w2=T(v2) then w1+cw2=T(v1+cv2) is also in the image. ∎
For a matrix map TA, the kernel is the null space N(A) and the image is the column space C(A) from Linear Algebra 02.
Proposition 3. T is injective if and only if ker⁡T={0}.
Proof. If T is injective and T(v)=0=T(0), then v=0. Conversely, if ker⁡T={0} and T(u)=T(v), then T(u−v)=0, so u−v=0. ∎
Watch out: "The only solution of T(v)=0 is v=0" is a statement about one equation, but it controls every equation T(v)=w: each one then has at most one solution. This is the map version of "no free variables" from Linear Algebra 00.

Linear Algebra 02 proved rank⁡A+dim⁡N(A)=n for an m×n matrix by counting pivot and free columns. Here is the version for maps, with a proof that uses no matrices at all.
Theorem 4 (rank–nullity). Let V be finite-dimensional and T:V→W linear. Then im⁡T is finite-dimensional and
dim⁡V=dim⁡ker⁡T+dim⁡im⁡T.
Proof. ker⁡T is a subspace of the finite-dimensional space V, so it has a basis u1,…,uk (possibly k=0). By the basis-extension theorem of Linear Algebra 02, extend it to a basis u1,…,uk,w1,…,wr of V, so dim⁡V=k+r. We show that T(w1),…,T(wr) is a basis of im⁡T; then dim⁡im⁡T=r and we are done.
Spanning. Any vector in the image is T(v) for some v=∑aiui+∑bjwj. Since T(ui)=0, we get T(v)=∑bjT(wj).
Independence. Suppose ∑cjT(wj)=0. Then T(∑cjwj)=0, so ∑cjwj∈ker⁡T and can be written as ∑diui. Then ∑cjwj−∑diui=0 is a linear relation among the basis vectors of V, so every cj (and every di) is zero. ∎
Worked example. T:R3→R2, T(x,y,z)=(x+2y−z, 2x+4y+z). Its matrix is
A=(12−1241).
Solving T(v)=0: adding the two equations gives 3x+6y=0, so x=−2y, and then z=x+2y=0. The kernel is the line spanned by (−2,1,0), so the nullity is 1. Rank–nullity forces dim⁡im⁡T=3−1=2, so the image is all of R2: T is surjective but not injective.
Worked example (no matrix in sight). D:P3→P2, D(p)=p′. The kernel is the constant polynomials (dimension 1). Every q∈P2 is the derivative of some cubic, so the image is P2 (dimension 3). Check: 4=1+3.

Corollary 5. Let T:V→W be linear with V,W finite-dimensional.
If dim⁡V>dim⁡W, then T is not injective (the kernel has dimension at least dim⁡V−dim⁡W>0).
If dim⁡V<dim⁡W, then T is not surjective (the image has dimension at most dim⁡V).
If dim⁡V=dim⁡W, then T injective ⟺ T surjective ⟺ T is an isomorphism.
Proof of 3. Injective means dim⁡ker⁡T=0, which by rank–nullity means dim⁡im⁡T=dim⁡V=dim⁡W, which means im⁡T=W (a subspace of full dimension is the whole space). ∎
Part 3 is the abstract form of the invertible matrix theorem from Linear Algebra 01: for a square matrix, "only the trivial solution" and "a solution for every right-hand side" are the same condition.
Theorem 6 (classification by dimension). Two finite-dimensional spaces are isomorphic if and only if they have the same dimension. In particular every n-dimensional real space is isomorphic to Rn.
Proof. An isomorphism sends a basis to a basis (it is injective, so independence is kept, and surjective, so the images span), so dimensions agree. Conversely, if dim⁡V=n with basis b1,…,bn, the coordinate map v↦(c1,…,cn) is linear, injective and surjective. Composing two such maps gives V≅Rn≅W. ∎
The inverse of an isomorphism is automatically linear: if T(u′)=u and T(v′)=v, then T(u′+cv′)=u+cv, so T−1(u+cv)=T−1(u)+cT−1(v).
Common pitfall: Isomorphic does not mean equal. P2 and R3 are isomorphic, but the isomorphism depends on a choice of basis. There is no single "correct" identification — which is exactly why the next chapter keeps track of bases.

Fix an ordered basis B=(b1,…,bn) of V. The coordinate vector of v is the column [v]B=(c1,…,cn)T with v=∑cibi. The map v↦[v]B is the isomorphism V→Rn of Theorem 6. Order matters: swapping b1 and b2 swaps the first two coordinates.

Let T:V→W be linear, with basis B=(b1,…,bn) of V and C=(c1,…,cm) of W. The matrix of T relative to B and C is the m×n matrix
[T]C←B=([T(b1)]C [T(b2)]C ⋯ [T(bn)]C).
Column j = the C-coordinates of the image of the j-th basis vector. With it, applying T becomes matrix multiplication on coordinates:
[T(v)]C=[T]C←B [v]B.
Why: if v=∑xjbj then T(v)=∑xjT(bj), and taking C-coordinates (a linear operation) gives ∑xj[T(bj)]C, which is the matrix times the column x.
The arrow notation C←B reads right to left: coordinates in B go in, coordinates in C come out. When V=W and the same basis is used on both sides, write [T]B.
Worked example. D:P3→P2 with bases (1,x,x2,x3) and (1,x,x2). The images of the basis vectors are 0, 1, 2x, 3x2, whose coordinates are the columns:
[D]=(010000200003).
Check with p=1+2x−x2+4x3: [D] (1,2,−1,4)T=(2,−2,12)T, and indeed p′=2−2x+12x2. The matrix has rank 3 and a one-dimensional null space spanned by (1,0,0,0)T — the constant polynomial 1 — matching the rank–nullity count above.

Theorem 7. Let T:U→V and S:V→W be linear, with bases B,C,D of U,V,W. Then
[S∘T]D←B=[S]D←C [T]C←B.
Proof. For every u∈U: [S(T(u))]D=[S] [T(u)]C=[S] [T] [u]B. Taking u=bj (so [u]B is the j-th standard column) shows that column j of [S∘T] equals column j of [S][T]. ∎
This is why matrix multiplication is defined the strange row-times-column way: it is the only definition that makes "do T, then do S" correspond to a product. It also explains why the product is associative (composition of functions is) and generally not commutative (doing things in a different order usually gives a different result). The order is right to left: in ST, T acts first.
Two consequences follow at once. T is an isomorphism if and only if its matrix (in any bases) is invertible, and then [T−1]B←C=([T]C←B)−1. And the rank of T equals the rank of any matrix that represents it.

Let E be the standard basis of Rn and B=(b1,…,bn) another basis. Put the new basis vectors, written in standard coordinates, into the columns of
P=PE←B=(b1 b2 ⋯ bn).
Then v=∑cibi=P [v]B, that is
[v]E=P [v]B,[v]B=P−1[v]E.
P is invertible because its columns are a basis. P is simply the matrix of the identity map, [id]E←B: it takes B-coordinates in and gives E-coordinates out.
Common pitfall: The matrix whose columns are the new basis vectors converts new coordinates to old, not old to new. To get new coordinates you must solve Pc=v (or apply P−1). Writing the arrow E←B on every change-of-basis matrix prevents this mistake.

Let T:Rn→Rn have standard matrix A=[T]E. Its matrix in the basis B is found by composing: convert B-coordinates to standard (P), apply T (A), convert back (P−1):
[T]B=P−1AP.
This is Theorem 7 applied to T=id∘T∘id. For a map between different spaces, with change-of-basis matrices P on the domain and Q on the codomain, the rule is [T]C′←B′=Q−1 [T]C←B P.
Worked example. Let A=(2112) and take the basis b1=(1,1), b2=(1,−1). Then
P=(111−1),P−1=12(111−1),P−1AP=(3001).
You can see the diagonal answer directly: Ab1=(3,3)=3b1 and Ab2=(1,−1)=b2. In the new basis the map just stretches the b1 direction by 3 and leaves the b2 direction alone. Now track one vector. v=(5,1) has [v]B=P−1v=(3,2), because 3(1,1)+2(1,−1)=(5,1). In new coordinates the map gives diag⁡(3,1) (3,2)T=(9,2)T, and 9(1,1)+2(1,−1)=(11,7)=Av. The two routes agree.
Choosing a basis that makes the matrix diagonal is the whole subject of Linear Algebra 04: b1 and b2 here are eigenvectors.

Square matrices A and B are similar if B=P−1AP for some invertible P. Similar matrices are the same linear operator written in two bases. Similarity is an equivalence relation (reflexive with P=I, symmetric with P−1, transitive with PQ).
Anything defined for the operator rather than the table of numbers must be the same for similar matrices. Such quantities are called similarity invariants:
Invariant · Why it survives A↦P−1AP
Rank · rank of the map, which does not depend on coordinates
Trace · tr⁡(XY)=tr⁡(YX), so tr⁡(P−1(AP))=tr⁡((AP)P−1)
Determinant · product rule (Chapter 6): det⁡P−1det⁡Adet⁡P=det⁡A
Characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues · Linear Algebra 04
The trace identity is a one-line calculation: tr⁡(XY)=∑i∑jxijyji=∑j∑iyjixij=tr⁡(YX). Check the example: tr⁡A=4=3+1.
Watch out: Equal invariants do not prove similarity. I=(1001) and (1101) have the same rank, trace and determinant, but only I is similar to I (because P−1IP=I for every P).

The quickest way to read a 2×2 matrix: its columns are where e1=(1,0) and e2=(0,1) land. Draw those two arrows and you have drawn the map, because the unit square goes to the parallelogram they span and every grid line goes to a parallel grid line.
Map · Matrix · What it does · det
Rotation by θ · (cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ) · turns every vector by angle θ counter-clockwise · 1
Reflection in the line at angle θ · (cos⁡2θsin⁡2θsin⁡2θ−cos⁡2θ) · mirror image; vectors on the line stay put · −1
Shear · (1k01) · slides each point sideways by k times its height · 1
Projection onto the line at angle θ · (cos⁡2θcos⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θsin⁡θsin⁡2θ) · drops each point perpendicularly onto the line · 0
Scaling · (a00b) · stretches x by a and y by b · ab
Where these come from:
Rotation. e1 goes to (cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ) and e2 (at angle 90°) goes to (cos⁡(θ+90°),sin⁡(θ+90°))=(−sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ). For θ=30° this gives (3/2−1/21/23/2).
Projection. With the unit vector u=(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ) along the line, the projection of x is (u⋅x) u=(uuT)x, and uuT is the matrix in the table. It satisfies P2=P: projecting twice is the same as projecting once.
Reflection. Reflection = 2× projection − identity (go to the line, then the same distance again). Using 2cos⁡2θ−1=cos⁡2θ and 2sin⁡θcos⁡θ=sin⁡2θ gives the table entry. It satisfies F2=I.
Composition does not commute. Let R be rotation by 90° and F reflection in the x-axis:

= 2× projection − identity (go to the line, then the same distance again). Using 2cos⁡2θ−1=cos⁡2θ and 2sin⁡θcos⁡θ=sin⁡2θ gives the table entry. It satisfies F2=I.
Composition does not commute. Let R be rotation by 90° and F reflection in the x-axis:
R=(0−110),F=(100−1),FR=(0−1−10),RF=(0110).
"Rotate, then reflect" (FR) is the reflection in the line y=−x; "reflect, then rotate" (RF) is the reflection in y=x. Two different maps.
A projection is diagonal in the right basis. The projection onto the line y=2x has standard matrix 15(1224). In the basis (1,2),(−2,1) — one vector along the line, one perpendicular to it — its matrix is (1000): keep the first coordinate, kill the second. Same map, much clearer matrix.

Multilinear (in the rows) — linear in each row separately when the other rows are held fixed.
Alternating — the value is 0 whenever two rows are equal.
Permutation of {1,…,n} — a bijection σ of the set to itself; Sn is the set of all n! of them.
Sign sgn⁡(σ) — +1 if σ is a product of an even number of swaps, −1 if odd. Equivalently (−1)number of inversions, where an inversion is a pair i<j with σ(i)>σ(j).
Minor Mij — the determinant of the (n−1)×(n−1) matrix left after deleting row i and column j. Cofactor Cij=(−1)i+jMij.

For 2×2 matrices you know det⁡(abcd)=ad−bc. The clean way to generalise is not to guess a formula but to list the properties we want and prove that exactly one function has them.
A function D from n×n matrices to R is a determinant function if:
(Multilinear) D is linear in each row: D(…,u+cv,… )=D(…,u,… )+c D(…,v,… ), other rows fixed.
(Alternating) D(A)=0 if two rows of A are equal.
(Normalised) D(I)=1.
Theorem 8 (existence and uniqueness). There is exactly one determinant function, written det⁡. Moreover, any function D satisfying axioms 1 and 2 (but not necessarily 3) equals D(I)⋅det⁡.
Existence is shown by checking that the Leibniz formula below satisfies the three axioms; uniqueness follows because the axioms alone determine the value on every matrix, as the row-operation rules show. A full proof is in Axler (Chapter 9) or Hoffman and Kunze (Chapter 5); here we state it and use it.

From the axioms alone:
Swapping two rows changes the sign. Put u+v in both rows i and j. By axiom 2 the value is 0; expanding with axiom 1 gives D(u,u)+D(u,v)+D(v,u)+D(v,v)=0 (other rows omitted), and the first and last terms are 0, so D(u,v)=−D(v,u).
Scaling one row by c multiplies the determinant by c (axiom 1).
Adding a multiple of one row to another leaves the determinant unchanged: D(…,u+cv,…,v,… )=D(…,u,…,v,… )+c D(…,v,…,v,… ), and the last term is 0.
A zero row gives determinant 0 (scale that row by 0).
A triangular matrix has determinant = product of its diagonal entries. If all diagonal entries are nonzero, row replacements clear the off-diagonal entries without changing D, leaving a diagonal matrix, and axiom 1 plus axiom 3 give the product. If a diagonal entry is zero, elimination produces a zero row, so both sides are 0.
These rules are also the fastest way to compute: row-reduce to triangular form, keeping track of swaps and scalings.

Leibniz formula.
det⁡A=∑σ∈Snsgn⁡(σ) a1σ(1) a2σ(2)⋯anσ(n).
Each term picks one entry from every row and every column. For n=2 there are two terms, a11a22−a12a21. For n=3 there are six:
det⁡A=a11a22a33+a12a23a31+a13a21a32−a13a22a31−a11a23a32−a12a21a33.
Cofactor (Laplace) expansion along row i or column j:
det⁡A=∑j=1naijCij(row i),det⁡A=∑i=1naijCij(column j).
The signs (−1)i+j follow a checkerboard starting with + in the top-left corner. Expand along the row or column with the most zeros.
Worked example — three ways. Let
M=(1234567810).
Cofactor expansion along row 1:
det⁡M=1(5⋅10−6⋅8)−2(4⋅10−6⋅7)+3(4⋅8−5⋅7)=1(2)−2(−2)+3(−3)=−3.
Leibniz, six terms: 50+84+96−105−48−80=230−233=−3.
Elimination: R2−4R1 and R3−7R1 give rows (0,−3,−6) and (0,−6,−11); then R3−2R2 gives (0,0,1). Only row replacements were used, so the determinant is unchanged: det⁡M=1⋅(−3)⋅1=−3.
Watch out: The "diagonals" trick (rule of Sarrus) works for 3×3 matrices only. For 4×4 it gives 8 terms, but the determinant has 4!=24.

Theorem 9. det⁡(AB)=det⁡A⋅det⁡B for all n×n matrices A,B.
Proof. Fix B and define D(A)=det⁡(AB). Row i of AB is (row i of A) ×B, which is linear in row i of A, so D is multilinear in the rows of A. If A has two equal rows, so does AB, so D(A)=0. By the second part of Theorem 8, D(A)=D(I)det⁡A=det⁡(B)det⁡(A). ∎
Theorem 10. det⁡AT=det⁡A.
Reason. In the Leibniz formula, the term for σ in det⁡AT is the term for σ−1 in det⁡A, and sgn⁡(σ−1)=sgn⁡(σ). As σ runs over Sn so does σ−1. ∎
So every statement about rows also holds for columns: column swaps flip the sign, and so on.
Theorem 11 (the invertibility test). A square matrix A is invertible if and only if det⁡A≠0. In that case det⁡(A−1)=1/det⁡A.
Proof. Row-reduce: Ek⋯E1A=R with R in reduced row echelon form. Each elementary operation multiplies the determinant by a nonzero number (−1, c≠0, or 1), so det⁡A≠0 ⟺ det⁡R≠0. A square RREF is either I (determinant 1) or has a zero row (determinant 0), and R=I exactly when A is invertible (Linear Algebra 01). For the formula, det⁡Adet⁡A−1=det⁡I=1. ∎
Further consequences:
det⁡(cA)=cndet⁡A for an n×n matrix (each of the n rows is scaled). For the matrix M above, det⁡(2M)=8⋅(−3)=−24.
Similar matrices have equal determinants, so det⁡T is well defined for a linear operator T: use its matrix in any basis.
For block upper triangular matrices, det⁡(AB0D)=det⁡Adet⁡D (with A, D square).
Common pitfall: det⁡(A+B)≠det⁡A+det⁡B in general. Try A=B=I2: the left side is det⁡(2I)=4, the right side is 2. The determinant is multiplicative, not additive.

For n×n A with columns a1,…,an, the number ∣det⁡A∣ is the volume (area when n=2) of the parallelepiped {t1a1+⋯+tnan:0≤ti≤1}.
Why this is plausible: signed volume, as a function of the edge vectors, satisfies the axioms. Scaling one edge by c scales the volume by c. Sliding one edge along another (a shear) does not change the volume — Cavalieri's principle, the same reason a slanted stack of coins has the same volume as a straight one. Two equal edges give a flat box of volume 0. The unit cube has volume 1. By uniqueness, signed volume is the determinant.
Since A sends the unit cube (volume 1) to this parallelepiped, and the map is linear, A multiplies the volume of every region by ∣det⁡A∣. This is the factor ∣det⁡J∣ in the change-of-variables formula for multiple integrals. The sign records orientation: det⁡A>0 keeps the order of the edges (counter-clockwise stays counter-clockwise in the plane), det⁡A<0 reverses it, as a mirror does. det⁡A=0 means the space is flattened into a lower dimension — and that information cannot be undone, which is Theorem 11 seen geometrically.
Example in R3: the columns (1,0,0), (1,2,0), (1,1,3) form an upper triangular matrix with determinant 1⋅2⋅3=6, so the box they span has volume 6.
The figure uses A=(2112) (det⁡=3), the same matrix with its columns swapped, B=(1221) (det⁡=−3), and C=(2121) (det⁡=0). A and B produce the same parallelogram, but in B the image of e1 has moved to the other side of the image of e2: the turn from the first column to the second is clockwise, so the orientation is reversed. That is the column-swap rule, drawn.

Theorem 12 (Cramer's rule). If det⁡A≠0, the unique solution of Ax=b is
xi=det⁡Ai(b)det⁡A,i=1,…,n,
where Ai(b) is A with column i replaced by b.
Proof. Let Ii(x) be the identity matrix with column i replaced by x. Then A Ii(x)=Ai(b): its columns are Ae1,…,Ax,…,Aen, which are the columns of A with b=Ax in position i. Expanding det⁡Ii(x) along row i gives xi. The product rule then gives det⁡A⋅xi=det⁡Ai(b). ∎
Worked example. 2x+y=5, x+3y=10. Here det⁡A=6−1=5, and
x=det⁡(51103)5=55=1,y=det⁡(25110)5=155=3.
Check: 2+3=5 and 1+9=10.
The adjugate. Applying Cramer's rule to each column of AX=I gives an explicit inverse:
A−1=1det⁡Aadj⁡(A),adj⁡(A)ij=Cji.
Note the transpose: entry (i,j) of the adjugate is the cofactor at (j,i). For 2×2 this is the familiar (abcd)−1=1ad−bc(d−b−ca). For M above,
adj⁡(M)=(24−32−116−36−3),M−1=−13adj⁡(M)=(−2/3−4/31−2/311/3−21−21).

Cramer's rule is valuable for theory: it shows that each xi is a rational function of the entries of A and b, so the solution depends continuously (indeed smoothly) on the data wherever det⁡A≠0. As an algorithm it is a bad choice:
The Leibniz formula has n! terms. For n=20 that is 20!=2 432 902 008 176 640 000≈2.4×1018 products for a single determinant.
Even computing each determinant by elimination, Cramer needs n+1 determinants, each costing about as much as one full LU factorisation (≈23n3 flops). Gaussian elimination solves the system with one factorisation.
Determinants are poor measures of numerical trouble. det⁡(0.1 I100)=10−100, yet 0.1 I is perfectly well-behaved. Closeness to singularity is measured by the condition number (Linear Algebra 05 and the planned numerical post), not by the size of det⁡A.
Trick: In practice, a determinant is computed from an LU factorisation with partial pivoting, PA=LU: det⁡A=±∏uii, the sign coming from the number of row swaps. This is exactly the elimination method above.

2. Let E:P2→R2, E(p)=(p(0),p(1)). Find the kernel and image and check rank–nullity.
Solution
p∈ker⁡E means p(0)=p(1)=0, so 0 and 1 are roots: p=c x(x−1). The kernel is spanned by x2−x, dimension 1. The image contains E(1)=(1,1) and E(x)=(0,1), which are independent, so the image is R2 (dimension 2). Check: dim⁡P2=3=1+2.
3. Prove: if T:V→W is linear and dim⁡V>dim⁡W, then some nonzero v has T(v)=0. Deduce that a homogeneous system with more unknowns than equations has a nonzero solution.
Solution
By rank–nullity, dim⁡ker⁡T=dim⁡V−dim⁡im⁡T≥dim⁡V−dim⁡W>0, since im⁡T⊆W. A nonzero kernel contains a nonzero vector. For a system Ax=0 with A of size m×n, n>m, apply this to TA:Rn→Rm.

7. (Vandermonde) Show that det⁡(1aa21bb21cc2)=(b−a)(c−a)(c−b), and conclude that a quadratic through three points with distinct x-values is unique.
Solution
Subtract row 1 from rows 2 and 3 (determinant unchanged): rows become (0,b−a,b2−a2) and (0,c−a,c2−a2). Expand along column 1 and factor (b−a) and (c−a) out of the two rows: (b−a)(c−a)det⁡(1b+a1c+a)=(b−a)(c−a)(c−b). Fitting y=p0+p1x+p2x2 through (a,y1),(b,y2),(c,y3) is a linear system with exactly this matrix; if a,b,c are distinct the determinant is nonzero, so the solution exists and is unique.

Chapter 4 found a basis in which (2112) became diag⁡(3,1). Linear Algebra 04 turns that lucky find into a method. A vector that a map only stretches, Av=λv, is an eigenvector; the stretch factors are the roots of the characteristic polynomial det⁡(A−λI), which is where this post's determinant does its most important job. With enough eigenvectors, A=PDP−1 with D diagonal, and powers, Fibonacci numbers, Markov chains and systems of differential equations all become easy.
